Container.Name: codifier-mcp
Container.Overview: Self-hosted MCP server that keeps a project's rules in a SQLite registry instead of scattered Markdown files, and answers the question a chat cannot answer today: which rules am I under, right now. Rules are addressed to CONSUMERS (chats and skills) through named SCOPES, and the reading order is the breadth of the scope, so it stays correct on its own as consumers are added. History is written by database triggers, not by tool code, so a change made by hand is recorded too; nothing is ever deleted. A new rule reaches nobody until its batch is approved behind the admin code, against the batch's digest, and an approved rule is provisional and expires unless renewed. One database, many projects, each addressed by an opaque code. Access via OAuth 2.1 with GitHub login restricted to a single user, published by Tailscale Funnel.
Container.Requires: A GitHub OAuth application (free) and the Unraid Tailscale plugin with Funnel enabled. To approve rules you also need an ed25519 key pair, generated on your own machine: only the public half goes in here.

Config.Name: Web UI Port (published)
Config.Description: The port the administration UI is published on, on the server's own IP: you reach the page at http://SERVER-IP:9443/ like any other container of the house. This is a PORT MAPPING and the Web UI Port variable below is what the server listens on inside the container — two halves of one decision. Change one and change the other, or the page answers only inside the container and the failure looks exactly like a service that never started. The MCP port is NOT published here and must not be: it is served by the Tailscale Funnel, which runs alongside.

Config.Name: Database
Config.Description: The directory holding the registry database, on the server. It must be LOCAL storage — a pool or a disk — and never a network share: SQLite in WAL mode needs real file locking, and over SMB or NFS the locks are advisory at best. Backups (VACUUM INTO) are written in here too, under backup/. Everything in this directory is owned by root and readable by everyone: from the share you read it and you do not touch it, because a write by hand would bypass the triggers and break history in silence. Tip: give it a ZFS dataset of its own, so its snapshots are independent from the rest of the share.

Config.Name: App Data
Config.Description: Persistent service state: the OAuth tokens already issued (FASTMCP_HOME). It MUST live on a volume that survives container recreation — lose it and the client will ask you to authorise the connector all over again.

Config.Name: Tailscale State
Config.Description: The Tailscale node identity of this container. Lose it and the node comes back as new: the hostname changes, the Funnel needs re-authorisation and BASE_URL stops answering. One dedicated folder per container — sharing it with another container is the mistake that costs an afternoon. If Tailscale ever asks you to re-authorise during a normal update, that is not a step of the procedure: it is the symptom that this mount is missing.

Config.Name: Database Path
Config.Description: Full path of the database file INSIDE the container. Leave it as /db/rules.db: when you move the data you change the mount above, not this variable. One file holds ALL projects — the project is a column, not a database, so a new project needs no new container.

Config.Name: Backup Directory
Config.Description: Where rules_backup writes its copies (VACUUM INTO). A quiescent copy opens without recovery, and it is the one to take off-site. In WAL mode the database is THREE files, so copying just the .db by hand produces a corrupt backup — use the tool. ZFS snapshots remain the main safety net; this is the copy that leaves the house.

Config.Name: Provisional Days
Config.Description: How long an approved rule lives before it leaves the lists on its own. This is the mechanism that stops rules piling up: staying costs a decision, going is free. Renewal is not an opinion either — the rule records where it came from, so the question is simply whether it happened again. Ninety days is the default; shorter makes the review a chore, much longer makes it a formality.

Config.Name: Pending Proposals Cap
Config.Description: How many PENDING proposals a project may hold before rules_propose refuses, listing what is in the queue. The owner reads and decides in small batches — this number enforces that rhythm, and it used to be a rule until it died at the legislator's gate two: a machine-checkable constraint lives in the tool, not in the corpus. Approval and denial free the slots by themselves; there is no override flag, because an override would just be the extra proposal with extra steps. Optional, with a working default of 5 in the code: leave it empty unless you want a different rhythm.

Config.Name: Public URL
Config.Description: The full public URL the client uses to reach the service, e.g. https://host.your-tailnet.ts.net (no trailing slash). It must be https and must match EXACTLY what is registered in the GitHub OAuth application, scheme included: the callback there must be BASE_URL + /auth/callback. This is the most common first-run mistake. Startup is BLOCKED while this still reads CHANGEME.

Config.Name: GitHub Client ID
Config.Description: Client ID of the GitHub OAuth application. Create it at github.com under Settings, Developer settings, OAuth Apps, New OAuth App: Homepage = BASE_URL, Authorization callback URL = BASE_URL/auth/callback. USE A NEW APPLICATION FOR THIS SERVICE: do not recycle another container's, or the two will fight over the callback. Startup is BLOCKED while this still reads CHANGEME.

Config.Name: GitHub Client Secret
Config.Description: Client Secret of the same OAuth application. GitHub shows it ONCE, at generation time: if you lose it there is no recovery, you generate another and update it here. Startup is BLOCKED while this still reads CHANGEME.

Config.Name: Allowed GitHub Login
Config.Description: The only GitHub username allowed in. Anyone else who completes the login is refused on every MCP request, the handshake included, so from v1.2 they cannot even list the tools. This is the real front door: the project codes keep projects from finding each other by accident, they do not keep strangers out. Startup is BLOCKED while this still contains CHANGEME.

Config.Name: JWT Signing Key
Config.Description: The key the service uses to sign and encrypt the tokens it issues. GENERATE IT WITH: openssl rand -hex 32 (64 hex characters). It must stay STABLE over time: change it and every issued token becomes invalid, so you must disconnect and reconnect the connector. A different key per service, never reused, never regenerated out of habit. Startup is BLOCKED if it is shorter than 32 characters OR if it still looks like a placeholder — length alone was not enough, because a 64-character placeholder walked straight through and only failed at the first login.

Config.Name: Port
Config.Description: The listening port inside the container, and the same one the Funnel must publish (see Tailscale Serve Port below: the two MUST match, or preflight blocks startup). A different port per service if you run more than one.

Config.Name: Allowed IP Ranges
Config.Default: 160.79.104.0/21 # documented egress of the model provider
Config.Description: Defence in depth: a request is accepted only if its source IP falls inside one of these ranges. It does NOT replace OAuth, it adds to it. Since v1.2 the check runs on every MCP request and not only on tool calls, the handshake included — so a range that is wrong no longer shows up as a call that fails, it shows up as a connector that will not connect at all, and the line in the log saying which source was turned away is what tells that apart from a broken deployment. It does not cover the OAuth routes themselves: whoever is outside these ranges can still complete a login, they simply cannot speak MCP afterwards. SYNTAX: a semicolon separates the entries, a hash opens a description that runs to the end of the entry — the separator is not a comma exactly so that a description may contain one. Example: 160.79.104.0/21 # model provider egress ; 100.64.0.0/10 # tailnet, for a client of your own. An EMPTY string disables the filter entirely, which is useful only while testing locally. A malformed entry BLOCKS startup instead of being skipped: a filter wider or narrower than you believe is the kind of failure nobody notices, so preflight refuses to start and the log prints what it UNDERSTOOD, not what it was given. The older name ANTHROPIC_CIDR is deprecated but still honoured.

Container.Config: 160.79.104.0/21 # documented egress of the model provider

Config.Name: Log Level
Config.Description: How much the service says about itself. It governs ONLY this service's own logger, and that limit is the point: the root logger stays at WARNING, so a library never starts talking on our behalf; uvicorn's access log is pinned at WARNING as well, because one line per request slowly becomes a record of who asked what and when, and the arguments here are project codes; and fastmcp's own logger follows FASTMCP_LOG_LEVEL, which is set inside the image. INFO prints, once, what was found at boot: the registry line, with the engine version, the database and how many projects it holds, and the startup line, which carries the version and the whole resolved configuration. The startup line is what you read to confirm that an update actually took, so WARNING is the quiet setting for a service you have already watched come up. INFO also prints ONE line for every call a tool turns away — 'refused <tool>: <why>' — which is the thing to read the day somebody says the registry is refusing them, and the reason those refusals no longer arrive as thirty lines of traceback. That line carries consumer names, domains and malformed IDs — checked, not assumed: no project code and not the text that was searched for. It is not an access log even by accident, because it records only the calls that did NOT happen, which is useless as a register of what was consulted and is exactly what you need when diagnosing. Project codes do reach the log by another door that this knob does not close: fastmcp logs invalid arguments itself, at WARNING, with the arguments in the line. WARNING silences it, along with the two boot lines, and leaves everything that is a warning proper: the gate turning a stranger away, a wrong admin code, a schema rebuilt or migrated at open, and a LOG_LEVEL that had to be corrected. It does NOT silence the preflight, which prints on stdout and never passes through this logger — a run that fails still says why, whatever this is set to. And it never silences a FAULT: a broken machine keeps its full traceback at ERROR, which is the whole reason refusals and faults are told apart in the code rather than by how their message reads. The list is closed on purpose, at both ends and for different reasons. Below INFO there is nothing to switch on: this code contains no debug line at all, so DEBUG would behave exactly like INFO, and a knob that does nothing gets read as a knob that is broken. Above WARNING the gate's refusals disappear — and since v1.2 the gate covers the handshake, so that line is the only thing that tells a stranger turned away apart from a broken deployment: at the client the two look identical, the connector will not connect. The list is closed in the CODE too, not only in this dropdown, because a container built by hand has no template. Anything that is not INFO or WARNING falls back to INFO and says in the log what it rejected; WARN is understood as WARNING, since Python defines it as an alias and whoever writes it is asking for less noise, not more. A field left EMPTY is not a wrong value and is not reported: it means the same as not setting one, which is INFO. It has to fall back rather than refuse, because setLevel() raises on an unknown value and does so at import — that is, after the preflight has already printed a clean sheet, which is the worst place in the whole startup for a typo to land.

Config.Name: Web UI Port
Config.Description: The port the administration UI listens on INSIDE the container. Leave it empty and it is 9443, which is the value the code carries: a variable born later than its container has to have a working default, because Unraid does not propagate new variables to installations that already exist. If you change it, change the port mapping above to match — they are two halves of one decision, and the half you forget is the one that makes the page unreachable. Startup is BLOCKED on 443, 8443 and 10000: those are the only three ports Tailscale Funnel can publish, the Funnel runs in this container, and on one of them this page would be on the internet instead of on your LAN. Startup is also blocked if it is the same as the MCP port, because the second server to bind would die after the startup line had already said everything was fine.

Config.Name: Web UI Master Code
Config.Description: The password of the administration UI — the page where proposals are approved. It is the TWIN of the Admin Access Code and deliberately NOT the same secret: that one travels inside conversations, this one is typed in a browser and never leaves it. Minimum 12 characters; put it in your password manager, because there is no way to recover it and no second account. It is asked for at sign-in, and asked for AGAIN on every action that approves or denies — once per action, never once per rule, because a password typed four times in a row is typed without looking. Startup is BLOCKED while this still reads CHANGEME: without it the approval page would be open to whatever reaches the port.

Config.Name: Approvals Per Action
Config.Description: How many proposals the administration UI may approve in ONE action. It is the mechanical form of 'at the twelfth signature in a row a person signs without reading': past this number the page refuses the action whole and asks you to do it in more than one pass. Optional, with a working default of 5 in the code — which is also the default of the Pending Proposals Cap, so out of the box this ceiling never refuses anything: the queue has already stopped the sixth proposal at the door. It starts to matter the day you widen that queue, which is exactly the day it is worth having. Leave it empty unless you want a different rhythm.

Config.Name: Bind Host
Config.Description: The interface the server listens on inside the container. Leave it as 127.0.0.1: legitimate traffic arrives from the Funnel, which runs in the same container. Setting 0.0.0.0 exposes the service to the LAN without the Funnel's filtering.
